Q60747420.summary: At the centre of this walrus-ivory plaque, Christ sits enthroned within an oval mandorla, blessing with his right hand and holding a book, surrounded by the four living creatures: the angel and eagle above, the lion and ox below. Two tall winged figures holding books stand at either side. Once set on the side of a portable altar, the tiny relief has, as the curator who acquired it wrote, the monumentality of a great cathedral tympanum.
facts: This is the central plaque of three showing Christ in Majesty and the apostles, which the Cleveland Museum says were the first major acquisition of William M. Milliken, its first curator of decorative arts and later director.
Milliken recalled that the Christ in the mandorla 'could have been enlarged and would have graced the tympanum of a great cathedral'.
The plaque is only about 5.1 × 10.8 cm.

Q60747420.notes: The museum's title speaks of Christ and the Apostles (the apostles are on the flanking plaques); the two figures beside Christ on this plaque appear to be winged, i.e. angels. Retitled accordingly; the editors may prefer to keep the museum's title.

commons:201323990.summary: Christ sits within a great diamond-shaped glory, robed in red, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a jewelled book, with the words 'Alfa et Ω' and 'Initium et Finis' (the beginning and the end) written beside him. Above, two six-winged seraphim spread their feathers, and below stand the archangels Michael and Gabriel, each named, while a Latin inscription runs round the frame. The page proclaims Christ as Lord of all creation in the bold, flat colours of Spanish manuscript painting.
facts: The Codex Vigilanus (or Albeldensis) was compiled at the Riojan monastery of San Martín de Albelda by the monks Vigila, Sarracino and García and completed in 976.
Its illuminations combine Visigothic, Mozarabic and Carolingian elements; a copy, the Codex Aemilianensis, was made at San Millán de la Cogolla in 992.
The codex is a vast compilation including the canons of the Visigothic councils and the Liber Iudiciorum, and contains one of the earliest mentions of Arabic numerals in the West.
commons:201323990.notes: The Commons source (vallenajerilla.com) labels the image as from the Codex Albeldense/Vigilano but gives no folio, and the date range 976–992 on Commons spans both the Vigilanus (976) and its copy the Codex Aemilianensis (992); both are in the Escorial. The attribution to the Vigilanus specifically was not independently confirmed, so date has been left as 976–992.
